sources.title: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
sources.venue: arXiv preprint, cs.SE; no peer-reviewed venue established in the accessed record
sources.publication_status: preprint, v3 dated 29 September 2026; arXiv record only, publication status unknown
sources.access_level: full HTML text via linked alphaXiv rendering plus arXiv metadata/abstract
sources.content_locator: Abstract lines 16–18; study conditions and results in paper sections summarized at alphaXiv lines 27–43

findings.claim: Evidence does not justify defaulting to multi-agent debate as the way to discover useful alternatives: in a peer-reviewed benchmark study, debate protocols did not reliably outperform self-consistency or ensembles, though tuning some protocols improved results and made them sensitive to settings.
findings.decision_implication: Have investigators independently formulate a concern or alternative and attach evidence; use a short targeted challenge/review only when it probes a named disagreement. Compare against a simpler single-investigator baseline before institutionalizing debate rounds.
findings.assumptions: The coding investigation values grounded alternatives and decision utility rather than benchmark question accuracy alone.
findings.applicability_gap: The evaluated tasks/models are general reasoning benchmarks, not repository architecture investigations or the current mixed-model setting; abstract-level access limits method-level appraisal.
findings.next_discriminator: On a small matched set of real repository decisions, compare a scoped evidence brief with and without a single adversarial reviewer; measure expert-discovered useful alternatives, factual support, review time and cost.

findings.claim: For literature synthesis, retrieval of relevant passages, attribution, iterative retrieval-based verification, and evaluation of citations/coverage/factual correctness are empirically useful components; OpenScholar reports gains for an 8B model and a GPT-4o-backed pipeline on its ScholarQABench tasks.
findings.support_locator: Abstract and Introduction; Nature article lines 68–71, 91–111
findings.decision_implication: A practical subagent report should identify exact source passages for claims, distinguish evidence from inference, preserve conflicting evidence, and expose a cheap discriminator; treat citation checks as part of review rather than expecting fluent synthesis to be reliable.
findings.assumptions: The task's academic sources can be retrieved and inspected and the expert can independently inspect decisive sources.
findings.applicability_gap: OpenScholar uses a specialized corpus, retrievers/rerankers and iterative self-feedback; its QA benchmarks and models do not validate generic web research, repository claims, or smaller coding subagents. Not evidence that more synthesis iterations always help.
findings.next_discriminator: Audit a sample of submitted claims against cited source passages, tracking unsupported/misattributed claims and whether direct links let the architecture decision-maker resolve disagreements quickly.

findings.claim: Role-specialized multi-agent workflows have a positive but domain-limited published example: LiRA assigns outlining, subsection-writing, editing and reviewing roles and reports improved writing/citation quality on scientific review datasets.
findings.support_locator: Publisher abstract, lines 32–34; AAAI publication details lines 40–45
findings.decision_implication: If division of labor is used, specialize agents around concrete evidence tasks (e.g., causal assumption, alternative approach, counterevidence) and consolidate into a compact shared evidence record rather than simply adding agents or report length.
findings.assumptions: The tasks can be decomposed into independent questions whose outputs can be checked by a coordinator.
findings.applicability_gap: The source is about producing literature reviews, not architecture decisions; available here only at abstract/metadata level. It does not establish benefits for mixed-strength models, cost, or independent patch acceptance.
findings.next_discriminator: Compare a single broad repository investigation against two bounded, disjoint evidence questions with one expert synthesis; judge novel actionable findings and time to decision.

findings.claim: Repository exploration should be treated as a retrieval/selection problem with observable quality dimensions: ContextBench evaluates context precision, recall and efficiency and reports a gap between explored and used context, with elaborate scaffolding yielding only marginal retrieval gains in its evaluation.
findings.support_locator: Abstract, lines 3–4; cost observation at line 160
findings.decision_implication: Ask for a small number of decisive paths/symbols, callers, contrary evidence, and an explicit excluded-scope note; judge whether evidence was used to answer the decision, not how much source material was collected.
findings.assumptions: Repository investigation evidence can be inspected and mapped to the decision question.
findings.applicability_gap: This is a 2026 arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed status verified here; it benchmarks issue-resolution context retrieval with frontier LLMs, not architectural alternative discovery by lower-tier models.
findings.next_discriminator: For actual investigations, sample whether cited source locations are decision-relevant and whether any consequential alternative was missed; track retrieval breadth and report size alongside expert utility.

findings.claim: Repository context files are not a guaranteed shortcut: a recent arXiv study across four agent/model configurations found generated context files did not significantly improve success and increased inference cost over 20% on average; repository overviews were not useful, while instructions for non-standard practices may still be useful.
findings.support_locator: arXiv abstract lines 16–18; alphaXiv sections on conditions/results lines 27–43
findings.decision_implication: Do not treat a longer standing prompt or repository overview as an evidence substitute. Prefer task-specific questions and concise constraints; retain project instructions for local practices and evaluate added investigation guidance against actual decisions.
findings.assumptions: The report/prompt changes under consideration add context or task-specific guidance to repository agents.
findings.applicability_gap: Preprint only; tasks are issue patch completion on SWE-bench Lite and CTXbench, not investigation quality or architecture judgment. Some models/tasks may benefit, so this is a caution against assuming benefit, not proof of harm in this workflow.
findings.next_discriminator: Use a matched local evaluation of current versus proposed research prompt on the same repository questions, scoring supported alternatives, omissions, citation accuracy, review effort and cost.

rejected_or_redundant.reason: Useful context that repository-level issue work spans multiple functions/files and is challenging, but it evaluates patch completion, not investigation/prompt workflows; the opened arXiv record exposed only the abstract and did not change the decision implications above.

rejected_or_redundant.item: Additional generic debate and multi-agent system studies surfaced in search
rejected_or_redundant.reason: Not pursued after the ICML benchmark supplied both negative and conditional-positive evidence directly relevant to whether debate should be the default; extra broad results would be redundant within the operation budget.

unresolved: No retrieved study directly tests whether lower-reasoning subagents discover better architecture alternatives in existing repositories under mixed-model coordination. The proposed workflow therefore needs a matched local evaluation.

The sources do not establish that any prompt method preserves prompt-injection resistance, expert access to decisive sources, independent patch acceptance, or timely consequential review; these remain explicit process constraints to retain and separately assess.

ContextBench and AGENTS.md findings are arXiv preprints in the accessed records; publication status may change. LiRA and MAD full papers were not opened, so their reported results are bounded to publisher abstracts and metadata.
stop_reason: Decision-relevant evidence obtained across peer-reviewed debate and literature-synthesis studies, a peer-reviewed multi-agent writing example, and current repository-specific preprints. Remaining operation budget was not spent because additional broad searches were unlikely to resolve the key direct-applicability gap; stopped at 14 of 16 operations, before the 12-minute target.
escalation_ready: Yes. For Sol/Astra: existing evidence supports a narrow, task-specific, claim-to-passage investigation format and evaluation of actual decision utility; it does not establish an architecture or prompt change. Avoid adding debate or repository overview context by default. A practical discriminator is a matched evaluation on real repository architecture questions, scoring actionable supported alternatives, decision impact, omission rate, citation accuracy, expert review time/cost, while preserving direct-source review, independent patch acceptance, injection boundaries and timely escalation.
